name: Adam Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for giving me your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach history at Al-Huda Academy, a faith secondary school with about 600 pupils, and this is my second year. I'm in by quarter to eight, we have a short assembly, then I teach four or five lessons, mostly Year 7 to Year 9: the Normans, the Tudors, the Industrial Revolution. I also cover a bit of religious studies when they're short. I like it when a quiet kid asks a question that shows they've actually been thinking.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Behaviour, sometimes, with Year 9 boys after lunch. And I'm not quick with the computer side: the online register, the seating plans, the reports. I write my lesson plans in a notebook first, then type them up. My fiancée Samira laughs at me for it, but it's how I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people always get excited about the next gadget. At work I'd say teaching is about the relationship between a teacher and a pupil, and that hasn't changed in a thousand years. I wouldn't post anything; I'm not on social media much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. My school is steady, the parents are loyal, and the community values having teachers who share their faith and values. I've got about four months of money saved. The thing on my mind is the wedding next summer and finding a flat, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, notebook and all. I'd keep saving £300 a month towards the wedding and a deposit. Maybe I'd learn the online register system properly, because my head of department has asked me twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the wedding. How big a cost is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About £8,000, with both families helping. My father and Samira's father are paying for most of the food, which is the biggest part. Samira and I are covering the hall and the photographer, so that's where my savings go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the job worry you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only whether I'm getting better fast enough. My first-year observation said my lessons were too teacher-led, too much of me talking. I'm working on it, slowly.

say: I'd say people always get excited about the **next gadget**.
I'd say teaching is a **relationship** that hasn't changed in a thousand years.
think: My school is **steady** and the community values teachers who share its faith.
The **wedding** and finding a flat matter more to me than AI.
do: Keep planning lessons in a **notebook** as I do now.
Save **£300 a month** for the wedding and a deposit.
S0.quote: Teaching is about the relationship between a teacher and a pupil, and that hasn't changed in a thousand years.
fieldNote: His sense of safety comes from a **loyal community** and faith school.
His money is aimed at a **wedding next summer**, shared with both families.
He's honest that his **teaching skill** is still developing.

steps.text: Keep planning history lessons in a notebook first
Save £300 a month for the wedding hall and a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools shouldn't rush into it, and that children need real teachers, not screens. I'd probably say it at a staff meeting if it came up. I'd say parents chose our school because they want people, not programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit, because a lot of history teaching is reading, writing and marking essays, and that's what the card says AI takes over. If the trust that runs our school decided to save money, they might use AI for marking and planning and need fewer teachers. I'm the youngest in the humanities team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a colleague, Mr Bashir, who's good with computers, to show me the basics of the tools the school uses, just enough to keep up. I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more. I wouldn't change the wedding plans; that's family, and family comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like it, but I think I'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if posts were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the government, really. Schools have to balance their books like a business. I'd blame the people who sell these gadgets to schools as if they're magic, and the heads who buy them to look modern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn 'just enough'. Why not more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust it. If I start relying on AI for my lesson planning, I'll stop thinking for myself, and thinking is my job. I'd learn enough so nobody can say I refused, and no more.

say: I'd say schools **shouldn't rush** into AI, because children need real teachers.
I'd say parents chose our school for **people, not programs**.
think: History teaching is a lot of **reading and marking**, which AI could take.
I'm the **youngest** in the humanities team, so I'd go first.
do: Ask a colleague to show me **just enough** of the school's tools.
Keep saving and add a **little more** each month.
S1.quote: If I start relying on AI for my lesson planning, I'll stop thinking for myself, and thinking is my job.
fieldNote: He blames **gadget sellers** and image-conscious heads, not government.
His **family plans** stay fixed, whatever happens to the school.

steps.text: Ask Mr Bashir to show him the school's AI marking tool
Add £50 a month to his wedding and deposit savings
Keep the summer wedding date as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should slow down and think about what kind of world we want our children to grow up in. I'd say it at the mosque, at work and to family. I'd probably sign something, though I don't normally do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of my work could go. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, it can teach history facts and mark essays better than me. What's left is the character side: discipline, values, being a role model. I think a faith school would keep that longer, but I'm not sure they'd keep me, a second-year teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the head if I could take on more pastoral work and religious studies, because those are about values. I'd still get married, but we'd have a smaller wedding, maybe £5,000 instead of £8,000, and put the rest aside. And I'd talk to my uncle, who runs a building firm, about whether there's work if teaching goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a heavy feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the robot date, three years later, change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my uncle's offer real. If thinking work goes in 2028 but hands-on work lasts until 2031, then building is safer than teaching for a while. I never thought I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Samira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'll be fine, because we have family. Her family and mine would help, and we'd help them. That's how we've always managed, not by waiting for the government.

say: I'd ask what world we want our **children** to grow up in.
I'd speak up at the **mosque**, at work and in the family.
think: Much of my **thinking work** could go by 2028.
A faith school might keep **character teaching**, but not necessarily me.
do: Ask for more **pastoral and religious studies** work.
Cut the wedding budget from **£8,000 to £5,000**.
Ask my uncle about work at his **building firm**.
S2.quote: If thinking work goes in 2028 but hands-on work lasts until 2031, then building is safer than teaching for a while.
fieldNote: He turns to **family and community**, not government, for support.
The 2031 robot date makes his uncle's **building firm** an option.
He'd **shrink the wedding** but not delay it.

steps.text: Ask his uncle about labouring work at the building firm
Cut the wedding budget from £8,000 to £5,000
Lean on both families to share wedding and living costs
Keep next summer's wedding date but hold a smaller celebration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but with less alarm. Schools and families should use the time to protect what matters. I'd talk about it more with the older teachers and the imam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to get better and become more useful to the school. By 2031 I'd be in my seventh year. But I'm slow with change, I know that, so I'd probably waste the first year or two hoping it wasn't real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training in pastoral leadership, maybe a head of year role later. I'd get married next summer as planned and start saving for a deposit with Samira. I'd keep my uncle's offer in mind but not take it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I think, but steadier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste a year or two. What would wake you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a colleague lose their job. If one of the older teachers in our humanities team was let go, I'd know the change was real. Until then, I'd keep my head down and teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Samira think the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, she's quicker than me. She works in a pharmacy, and she already uses the computer systems more than I do. She'd push me, and she'd probably be right.

say: I'd say schools and families should **use the time**.
I'd talk more with **older teachers** and the imam.
think: Five years lets me **get better** and more useful to the school.
I'd likely **waste a year** or two hoping it wasn't real.
do: **Get married** next summer as planned and save for a deposit.
Keep my uncle's **building offer** in reserve.
S3.quote: If one of the older teachers in our humanities team was let go, I'd know the change was real.
fieldNote: His fiancée, a pharmacy worker, is **quicker with tech** and would push him.
He keeps a **fallback** in the family business.

steps.text: Ask the school for pastoral leadership training
Marry Samira next summer and start saving for a deposit
Wait to see whether older colleagues lose posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for schools to work out what really matters. I'd say teachers will be needed for character and values even if machines can teach facts. I'd say it with some confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'm thirty-seven when it lands. By then I'd hope to be a head of year in a faith school, and I think that's a role parents will want a person in. I'd worry about my own children, if we have them by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and focus on getting better at the pastoral side. Samira and I would get married, buy a small house around 2029, and maybe have our first child. I'd learn the tools slowly, when the school makes us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn a trade or a craft alongside school, something with their hands. And I'd want them to have strong values. In a world where machines can teach facts, character is what's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change your mind about staying in teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the school started replacing teachers with screens, I'd leave. I wouldn't want to be part of that. But I think a faith school would be one of the last to do it.

I'd say teachers are still needed for **character and values**.
think: By 2036 I'd hope to be a **head of year** in a faith school.
I'd worry about my own **future children**.
do: Focus on getting better at **pastoral work**.
Marry, **buy a small house** around 2029, and maybe have a child.
Learn the tools **slowly**, when the school requires it.
S4.quote: In a world where machines can teach facts, character is what's left.
fieldNote: Ten years makes **family plans** feel safe again.
He'd **leave** rather than help replace teachers with screens.
He'd push his future children towards a **trade or craft**.

steps.text: Keep teaching history and build pastoral skills

Plan for a first child after the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'm slow with change, and two years isn't enough for someone like me. What would help is schools being honest early, and families and communities supporting each other, like we do at the mosque. Apprenticeships too, for young people who need a different path.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For a lot of people I know, faith is what gets them through hard changes. In a world like the ones you described, I think people would turn back to it.

headlineQuote: For a lot of people I know, faith is what gets them through hard changes.
portrait: Adam is a second-year **history teacher** at a faith secondary school who plans lessons in a notebook.
He's **engaged**, saving for a wedding next summer with help from both families.
He distrusts AI and would learn it only **defensively**, relying on family and community instead.
He moves from **calm** to anxious, with a building-firm fallback from his uncle.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he's **slow with change** and two years is too short.
whatWouldHelp: Community support and **apprenticeships** for young people.
